analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay equally for jobs of equivalent skill, effort, and responsibility.
analysis.headline: The Fair Pay Act of 2023 died in committee without a single hearing or vote, after drawing only one cosponsor in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to bar employers from paying workers in female-, race-, or ethnic-dominated jobs less than workers in different but equivalent jobs — measured as a composite of skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions. It would allow compensatory and punitive damages, protect employees who discuss wages, and require employers with 25 or more workers (15 after two years) to report pay data by race and sex to the EEOC. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs dominated by women or by particular racial or ethnic groups who are paid less than workers in different jobs requiring equivalent skill, effort, and responsibility — for example, traditionally female jobs such as nursing support or teaching aides compared to traditionally male jobs of similar demands. The bill's findings cite estimates that women lose roughly $500 billion in combined wages each year to the gap, and that equal pay could roughly halve the poverty rate for working women.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in underpaid female- and minority-dominated jobs

how_it_helps.text: Requires equal pay for 'equivalent jobs' — jobs that may be dissimilar but whose requirements are equivalent as a composite of skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions, closing a gap left by the Equal Pay Act's narrower 'equal work' standard [S2] [S3].
Allows compensatory and punitive damages, expert fees, and class actions for violations, and treats withheld wages as unpaid minimum wages under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S2] [S3].
Makes it illegal to fire or retaliate against an employee for asking about, disclosing, or discussing anyone's wages, or for opposing or assisting an investigation of pay discrimination [S2] [S3].

Requires employers with 25 or more employees (15 or more after two years) to report pay rates by job classification along with employees' sex, race, and national origin to the EEOC, with confidentiality protections [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with pay disparities between equivalent jobs would owe back pay, plus compensatory and possibly punitive damages, and would face new recordkeeping and pay-reporting duties; firms might also bear litigation and job-valuation costs.

drawbacks.text: Comparing the worth of dissimilar jobs is inherently subjective, so the equivalent-jobs standard would likely generate extensive litigation over how to value skills, effort, and responsibility, and employers would face compliance and recordkeeping costs [S3].
The pay-data reporting requirement applies to employers with 25 or more employees in the first two years and 15 or more thereafter, an administrative burden on small and mid-sized firms [S3].

Employers can still pay different wages under seniority, merit, or production systems, or any bona fide job-related factor — but the bill lets employees challenge whether such a factor is a pretext, and bars employers from cutting anyone's wages to comply, which could force costly across-the-board adjustments [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a large, documented problem — the bill's own findings cite women being paid 80 cents on the dollar and far less for Black, Native, and Hispanic women — and gives workers real remedies. The honest cost is on the employer side: valuing dissimilar jobs is difficult, and the mandates would bring litigation, compliance spending, and reporting burdens that would fall hardest on firms with complex pay structures. Whether the equivalence standard can be administered fairly at scale is a genuine design question, not just an objection from the affected industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there; the committee never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2023 on March 14, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S1] [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor — a single House Democrat — in nearly two years [S4].
No further action of any kind appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced equivalent-job pay claims, punitive damages, and EEOC pay-data reporting were better off because the bill never advanced, while the pay disparities it targeted continued unchecked.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2023 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor [S1] [S5].

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-led committee that held the bill took no action on it.

industries.industry: Employers with pay disparities across equivalent jobs (retail, care work, service industries)
industries.note: The bill would have required equal pay for equivalent work and allowed compensatory and punitive damages, so employers with race-, sex-, or ethnicity-based pay gaps between different-but-equivalent jobs would owe back pay and face lawsuits. The bill's findings estimate the pay gap costs women roughly $500 billion a year, so the employer cost is the mirror image of worker gains [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Payroll, HR compliance, and workforce analytics services
industries.note: The bill's recordkeeping and pay-data reporting requirements — with EEOC-prescribed forms for employers with 25 or more employees — would create a compliance services market around documenting and reporting wage rates [S3].
